items.prompt: Define price elasticity of demand.
items.canonical_answer: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in its own price.
marking_guidance: The precise meaning must be present: the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the good's own price.
One mark for the measure named on the right quantities; one mark for tying it to the good's own price rather than to any other influence on demand.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Identify two features of price elasticity of demand that distinguish it from price elasticity of supply.
items.canonical_answer: PED measures how buyers respond - the change in quantity demanded - whereas PES (topic 2.8) measures how sellers respond through quantity supplied. PED's raw value is negative, as price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so it is quoted unsigned; PES is positive.
marking_guidance: Reward two features stated, one mark each: PED measures the response of quantity demanded by buyers, where PES measures quantity supplied by sellers; and PED's raw value is negative, quoted as an absolute value, where PES is positive.

What it includes: another genuine contrast, such as determinants rooted in buyers' substitutes and income share rather than producers' spare capacity and time, may take the second mark; restating the first feature in other words earns nothing more.

items.prompt: State the formula for price elasticity of demand.
items.canonical_answer: PED = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price. The result is quoted as an absolute value, without the minus sign, because price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.
marking_guidance: The precise meaning of the calculation: percentage change in quantity demanded over percentage change in price.
A full definition names both percentage changes and the division between them; the sign convention is worth noting but the division is the definition.

items.prompt: Kaoko Juice sells 200 bottles a week in Opuwo at N$10 a bottle, and its demand is price-elastic. Discuss how a demand diagram of this market shows the elasticity, giving a verbal walk-through of every part of the diagram and what it shows.
items.canonical_answer: Price of juice (N$ a bottle) goes on the vertical axis and quantity demanded (bottles a week) on the horizontal. One demand curve, D, is drawn relatively flat over this range to show elastic demand, with the point at N$10 and 200 bottles marked. A price rise to N$12 is a movement up along D, not a shift, because the juice's own price changed; mark the new point at N$12 and a quantity well below 200 bottles. The diagram shows elasticity as the size of the horizontal move against the vertical one: a 20 per cent price rise sends quantity demanded back by more than 20 per cent. The link is between the elasticity figure and the flat shape of the curve. The consequence falls on Kaoko Juice: with elastic demand the bottles lost outweigh the higher price, so revenue tends to fall, and a price cut would tend to raise it.
marking_guidance: The walk-through must name the axes labelled - price and quantity, each with its units - before anything else.
Reward the original curves drawn and labelled: the demand curve in place at N$10 and 200 bottles before the change is described, drawn to show a flat, responsive shape.
Check the shift or movement, in the correct direction: a change in the good's own price is a movement up an unchanged demand curve, not a shift of it.
The new point marked and labelled at the new price and its smaller quantity earns its mark, and what the diagram shows, in words, must close the walk-through.
The link between the elasticity figure and its drawn form, and the consequence for the seller's revenue - lost bottles outweighing the higher price - carry the analysis marks.

items.prompt: A stall in Walvis Bay tested its fresh-bread prices over four weeks, changing nothing else. At N$8 a loaf it sold 300 loaves; at N$9, 270 loaves; at N$10, 240 loaves; at N$11, 200 loaves. The stall also computed PED for each price step: 0.80, then 1.00, then 1.67. Explain what these figures show about the demand for the bread.
items.canonical_answer: The figures show demand becoming more price-elastic as the price climbs: PED rises from 0.80 (inelastic) through 1.00 (unit) to 1.67 (elastic). Each N$1 rise is a shrinking percentage of the price (12.5, 11.1, then 10.0 per cent), while the loaves lost (30, 30, then 40) are a growing percentage of a shrinking quantity (10.0, 11.1, then 16.7 per cent). At higher prices the remaining buyers are nearer their limit, so more drop out. However, 1.00 is a borderline, and four weeks is a small sample.
marking_guidance: What the data shows - elasticity rising as price rises along the same demand curve - must be stated first, with supporting evidence taken as a comparison across the three steps.
The exception or limit earns a mark: however, the unit point at 1.00 is a borderline, not a settled classification.
The why - an explanation of the relationship, through buyers near the edge of willingness to pay at high prices - is worth as much as the reading; quoting the elasticity figures alone earns nothing.

items.prompt: Etosha Gate Lodge raised its guided-drive price from N$150 a seat to N$180, and seats filled fell from 120 a week to 90. Using these figures, explain how the lodge should calculate and classify the elasticity of demand for its drives.
items.canonical_answer: Seats fell by 120 - 90 = 30, which is 30 / 120 x 100 = 25 per cent; the price rose by 180 - 150 = 30, which is 30 / 150 x 100 = 20 per cent. PED = 25 / 20 = 1.25, quoted without the minus sign. Because 1.25 is greater than 1, demand for the drives is price-elastic. So revenue fell, from N$18 000 (150 x 120) to N$16 200 (180 x 90): if revenue is the aim, the rise was a mistake.
marking_guidance: The context - the two percentage changes from the lodge's own figures - must be worked, not assumed: reasoning earns the marks because the percentages, not the raw counts, are what the formula divides.
The link from the classification to the revenue consequence - lost seats outweighing the higher price - must be made explicitly.
The conclusion - therefore the rise tends to lower revenue, given elastic demand - means that the answer is complete only with the classification stated as elastic.

items.prompt: A bus operator in Katima Mulilo computes the PED for its monthly ticket as 0.4 after a fare rise. Analyse what happens inside this market from the fare rise to the operator's revenue, naming who gains and who bears the cost.
items.canonical_answer: The fare is the good's own price, and a PED of 0.4 means demand is price-inelastic: the percentage fall in monthly tickets is only 0.4 times the percentage rise in the fare. Because quantity falls proportionately less than the fare rises, the higher fare times the remaining passengers gives more total revenue, so the operator gains. Commuters in Katima Mulilo have few other ways to travel, so most keep buying and bear the cost through higher spending on the same journeys, leaving less for other goods; the few who stop riding lose the service. The rise is mainly a transfer from commuters' budgets to the operator, and other local traders may see slightly less household spending.
marking_guidance: The starting point - the fare rise with an inelastic 0.4 - must open the chain, when the change is named as one in the good's own price.
The mechanism - the percentage fall in quantity demanded staying smaller than the percentage rise - is the link that earns the middle marks, because that is what makes the total rise.
The consequence - revenue rising for the firm - must be stated, and the transfer from consumer budgets to the operator named.
For whom: the consumer who keeps riding, the firm whose revenue rises, and the town households whose other spending is crowded - at least two parties named for full marks.

items.prompt: State two determinants of price elasticity of demand.
items.canonical_answer: Any two of: the availability and closeness of substitutes; the share of income the purchase takes; whether the good is a necessity or a luxury; how widely the market is defined; and the time since the price changed.
marking_guidance: The precise meaning: the market features that make demand more or less responsive to a price change.
Both marks need the list shaped as causes of responsiveness - substitutes, income share, necessity against luxury, market width, time - one mark for each of any two of the five.

items.prompt: A new supermarket opens beside a long-established bakery in Oshakati, stocking packaged bread at a lower price. Analyse how this change works through the determinants of PED to the bakery's sales, naming who gains and who loses.
items.canonical_answer: The supermarket's cheaper packaged bread is a new close substitute for the bakery's bread. Because closeness of substitutes is a main determinant of PED, demand for the bakery's bread becomes more price-elastic: buyers now have somewhere else to go. If the bakery raises its price, the percentage fall in its sales tends to be larger than before, so a rise that once raised revenue may now cut it. The effect tends to grow over time as habits fade. Consumers gain wider choice and pressure on the bakery's price; the supermarket gains the customers who switch; the bakery loses pricing power, and its workers may lose hours if it cuts costs, unless it makes its bread distinctive.
marking_guidance: The starting point - the substitute arriving - must open the chain, when the determinant named is substitutes.

The mechanism - demand becoming more elastic because the substitute sits beside the product - is the link that earns the middle marks, because elasticity is the channel between the shelf and the price.
The consequence - the bakery's price rises now tending to shrink revenue - must be stated.
For whom: the consumer, the bakery, its workers and the supermarket - at least two parties named, with the direction of the gain or loss stated for each.

items.prompt: A trader in the Katutura market sells matches at N$2 a box and also, from the same stall, handmade leather jackets at N$900. Explain, using the determinants of PED, why the elasticity of demand for these two goods is likely to differ.
items.canonical_answer: Matches at N$2 take a tiny share of income and are an everyday necessity, so even a large percentage price rise barely changes the household bill: demand tends to be price-inelastic. A N$900 jacket takes a large share of income and is a luxury that can be postponed, so demand tends to be price-elastic. So a dearer box of matches is likely to raise the trader's revenue from matches, because quantity falls little, while a dearer jacket is likely to lower revenue, as buyers wait or go elsewhere.
marking_guidance: The context - the N$2 against the N$900, the everyday necessity against the postponable luxury - is the data the reasoning must rest on.
Reasoning: because income share and necessity push towards inelastic demand for matches and towards elastic demand for jackets, with the because made explicit at each step.

The conclusion - therefore the trader's two goods carry different elasticities and the same pricing move works opposite ways on them - means that the answer must land on the contrast, not on each good separately.

items.prompt: A seller claims: "My product has no close substitutes, so my demand is inelastic, so I should raise my price." Discuss whether the seller's reasoning holds.
items.canonical_answer: On balance the first step holds but the conclusion does not follow automatically. For the seller: with no close substitutes demand tends to be price-inelastic, and where demand is inelastic a price rise tends to raise total revenue, because quantity demanded falls by a smaller percentage than the price rises. Against: other determinants may push the other way, since a product taking a large share of income, or a luxury, can have elastic demand even without substitutes. Substitutes also arrive over time, so demand tends to become more elastic as buyers adjust. And each rise moves the market up its demand curve, towards the stretch where demand tends to be elastic. What settles it is the PED measured at the new price, not the current one: if it stays below 1 the rise tends to pay; above 1, revenue falls. So the judgement depends on demand staying inelastic over the range of the rise.
marking_guidance: The judgement must come with its condition: demand being inelastic at the new price, not merely at the current one.
Why it might: the substitutes determinant giving inelastic demand, and inelastic demand making a rise pay - the argument for.
Why it might not: the other determinants, the arrival of substitutes over time, and the elastic stretch at higher prices - the argument against, at least two developed.
What settles it: the decisive test - the measured PED at the new price - named as the check that ends the argument.

items.prompt: Explain the features of a good whose demand is price-inelastic, and what each feature does to keep buyers buying.
items.canonical_answer: Each feature leaves buyers no easy way out. Few or distant substitutes mean a buyer cannot switch, as with clinic medicine in Gobabis. A small share of income, like N$2 matches, means a sharp percentage rise barely changes the budget. A necessity is bought even at a higher price. A widely defined market, such as all food rather than one bread brand, has fewer substitutes outside it. And soon after a rise, habits and contracts hold buyers in place.
marking_guidance: Reward the features: few substitutes, small income share, necessity, wide market definition, short time - what it includes for each is the mechanism that keeps buyers buying.
One mark per feature with its mechanism, up to four; naming the feature alone, without what it does to the buyer, is recall rather than explanation.

items.prompt: Define total spending on a product and state its link to the seller's revenue.
items.canonical_answer: Total spending by consumers on a product is the price multiplied by the quantity sold; the same figure is the seller's revenue from that product, because every dollar spent by buyers is a dollar received by the seller.
marking_guidance: The precise meaning: price times quantity, stated as the consumers' spending and identified with the seller's revenue.
Both marks need the multiplication named as the definition and the two sides of the same transaction - spending by buyers, revenue by seller - identified as one figure.

items.prompt: A rice trader in Windhoek faces price-inelastic demand for its sacks of rice. The trader raises the price from N$100 a sack to N$110, and quantity demanded falls only slightly. Discuss how a demand diagram of this market shows what happens to total spending, giving a verbal walk-through of every part of the diagram and what it shows.
items.canonical_answer: Price of rice (N$ a sack) goes on the vertical axis and quantity demanded (sacks a week) on the horizontal. One demand curve, D, is drawn steep over this range to show inelastic demand, with the point at N$100 marked. The rise to N$110 is a movement up along D, not a shift, because rice's own price changed; mark the new point at N$110 and a quantity only slightly smaller. Total spending at each point is the rectangle from the origin to that point: height the price, base the quantity. Moving up the curve makes the rectangle 10 per cent taller and only slightly narrower, because with inelastic demand quantity falls by less than 10 per cent. So the new rectangle is larger: total spending, which is the trader's revenue, rises. The link is between the inelastic classification and the rectangle's area; the consequence is more revenue for the trader, provided demand stays inelastic over the range of the rise, and more spending on rice by buyers.
marking_guidance: The walk-through must name the axes labelled - price and quantity, each with its units - before anything else.
Reward the original curves drawn and labelled: the demand curve in place at N$100 before the change is described, drawn to show a steep, unresponsive shape.
Check the shift or movement, in the correct direction: a rise in the good's own price is a movement up an unchanged demand curve, not a shift of it.
The new point marked and labelled at N$110 and its slightly smaller quantity earns its mark, and what the diagram shows, in words, must close the walk-through.

The link between the rectangle areas and the consequence for the trader's revenue - the taller rectangle winning with inelastic demand, provided demand stays inelastic over the range - carry the analysis marks.

items.prompt: A cinema in Swakopmund tested its ticket prices across four seasons, changing nothing else. At N$30, weekly spending on tickets was N$36 000; at N$40, it was N$44 000; at N$50, it was N$45 000; at N$60, it was N$42 000. Explain what these totals show about the elasticity of demand for cinema seats and why the pattern is not a straight line.
items.canonical_answer: Spending rises from N$36 000 at N$30 to N$44 000 at N$40 and N$45 000 at N$50, then falls to N$42 000 at N$60. Where a price rise lifts spending, quantity demanded fell by a smaller percentage than price, so demand is inelastic between N$30 and N$50. Where a rise cuts spending, demand is elastic, as between N$50 and N$60, where buyers are nearest their limit. Elasticity rises with price along the curve, so spending peaks and turns. However, near N$50 demand is close to unit elasticity, a borderline.
marking_guidance: What the data shows - spending rising with price at the low end and falling at the top - must be stated first, with supporting evidence taken as a comparison across the four totals.
The exception or limit earns a mark: however, the peak near N$50 is borderline ground where the classification tips either way.
The why - inelastic at the cheap end, elastic at the dear end, through the size of the percentage fall in quantity demanded - is worth as much as the reading; quoting the totals alone earns nothing.

items.prompt: Marula Foods sells dried marula snack packs in Oshakati at N$15 each and takes N$9 000 a week. A rival launches a similar pack at N$12, and Marula Foods' demand becomes price-elastic. Using these figures, explain what would happen to Marula Foods' weekly revenue if it raised its price to N$18, and why.
items.canonical_answer: Marula Foods sells 9000 / 15 = 600 packs a week. A rise to N$18 is 3 / 15 x 100 = 20 per cent. With elastic demand, sales fall by more than 20 per cent, to fewer than 480 packs, as the rival's N$12 pack offers an easy switch. Revenue would then be below 18 x 480 = 8640, under N$8 640 a week against N$9 000 now. The rise is therefore likely to lower revenue; holding or cutting the price fits elastic demand while the rival stays.
marking_guidance: The context - 600 packs at N$9 000, and the rival's N$12 pack - is the data the reasoning must rest on.
Reasoning: because the percentage fall in quantity demanded outweighs the percentage rise in price under elastic demand, with the because made explicit.
The conclusion - therefore the rise tends to lower revenue below N$9 000 - means that the answer is complete only with the direction stated and tied to the elastic classification.

items.prompt: A water utility serving Windhoek households raises its basic charge, and the demand for its water is price-inelastic. Analyse what follows for the utility's revenue and for the households, naming who gains and who bears the cost.
items.canonical_answer: The utility raises the price of water, and demand is price-inelastic: households need water for drinking, cooking and washing and have no close substitute. Because quantity demanded falls by a smaller percentage than the price rises, the higher charge times a nearly unchanged quantity gives higher total revenue, so the utility gains. Households bear the cost: they keep buying, so their bills rise and other spending is squeezed, hardest for low-income households, for whom water takes a larger share of income. The change is mainly a transfer from household budgets to the utility, and the same reliability is why governments find goods with inelastic demand a dependable tax base.
marking_guidance: The starting point - the charge rise with inelastic demand - must open the chain, when the change is named as one in the price.
The mechanism - the small percentage fall in quantity demanded against the larger percentage rise in price - is the link that earns the middle marks, because that is what makes the total rise.
The consequence - revenue rising for the utility, spending rising for the household - must be stated as a transfer.
For whom: the firm, the households whose budgets are squeezed, and the wider economy - at least two parties named, with the direction stated for each.

items.prompt: State why price elasticity of demand is significant for decision making.
items.canonical_answer: The effect of a price change on revenue depends on PED: with inelastic demand a price rise tends to raise revenue, with elastic demand it tends to lower it. So producers setting prices, and governments choosing goods to tax, are likely to weigh PED first.
marking_guidance: The precise meaning: elasticity deciding the revenue effect of a price change, which is why price-setters and tax-setters weigh it.
Both marks need the dependency named - the effect of a price change depends on elasticity - and at least one decision-maker, a producer or a government, identified as the one who weighs it.

items.prompt: Explain why a government choosing an indirect tax is likely to place it on goods whose demand is price-inelastic, and why the same reasoning points elsewhere when the purpose is to change behaviour.
items.canonical_answer: An indirect tax raises the price. Where demand is price-inelastic, quantity demanded falls by a smaller percentage than the price rises, so most units are still bought and the tax keeps collecting on them: a reliable source of revenue, which is why goods like fuel are common tax bases. If the purpose is to change behaviour, the reasoning reverses: a tax on a good with elastic demand cuts the quantity bought by a larger percentage, so consumption actually falls.
marking_guidance: Reward the reason: inelastic demand keeps quantity demanded close to unchanged, so the tax raises money on almost every unit - with the because made explicit.
The purpose of each choice must be named: revenue points at inelastic goods, behaviour change at elastic goods, and one mark sits on that contrast.

items.prompt: A lodge near the Etosha gate measures the demand for its off-season rooms as price-elastic. Using this measurement, explain how the lodge should set its off-season price, and what risk the measurement carries.
items.canonical_answer: Elastic demand means quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price. For off-season rooms, a price rise therefore tends to lower revenue and a price cut tends to raise it, because the extra guests more than make up for the lower rate. The lodge should set a lower off-season price. The risk is that PED is estimated from past data: if a new lodge opens or travel habits change, the figure may drift, so the decision rests on demand staying elastic through the off-season.
marking_guidance: The context - the measured elastic demand and the off-season setting - is the data the reasoning must rest on.
Reasoning: because demand is elastic, a cut tends to raise revenue through the extra guests outweighing the cheaper rate - with the because made explicit.
The conclusion - therefore a low off-season price - and the risk that the past measurement may drift, means that the answer must carry both the decision and the condition it rests on.

items.prompt: The demand for a good has a price elasticity of exactly 1. Define unit elasticity of demand.
items.canonical_answer: Unit elasticity of demand is where the percentage change in quantity demanded equals the percentage change in price, so PED = 1. Its demand curve bends towards the origin, with price multiplied by quantity the same at every point.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the percentage change in quantity demanded equals the percentage change in price, giving PED = 1; the curve shape supports the definition but does not replace it.

items.prompt: A hospital in Oshakati needs exactly 300 doses a week of an anti-venom drug and buys that number whatever the price. The supplier's costs rise, and the price of a dose rises from N$40 to N$60. Draw a demand-and-supply diagram of this market to show perfectly inelastic demand and the effect of the cost rise, and explain what it shows.
items.canonical_answer: Price (N$ a dose) goes on the vertical axis and doses a week on the horizontal. Demand D is a vertical line at 300 doses. S1 crosses D at E1, at N$40. The cost rise shifts supply left to S2, which crosses D at E2: N$60 and still 300 doses. The diagram shows the whole change landing on price: quantity demanded does not change, so PED = 0 / 50 = 0, and the hospital's spending rises from N$12 000 to N$18 000 a week.
marking_guidance: Axes labelled: price (N$ a dose) on the vertical axis and quantity (doses a week) on the horizontal.
Original curves drawn and labelled: a vertical demand curve D at 300 doses, crossed by S1 at E1, N$40.
The shift or movement, in the correct direction: the cost rise shifts supply left from S1 to S2, moving the market up the vertical demand curve.
New equilibrium marked and labelled at E2, N$60 and 300 doses.
What the diagram shows, in words: perfectly inelastic demand, PED = 0, so the price change leaves quantity demanded unchanged.

The link between the vertical curve and the outcome - buyers who take the same quantity at any price - and the consequence, N$20 more a dose and N$6 000 more spending a week, carry the analysis marks.

items.prompt: A maize grower near Grootfontein sells to a national mill that pays every grower N$5 000 a tonne for as much maize as they deliver, and buys none from a grower who asks more. Good rains raise the grower's harvest from 40 to 60 tonnes. Draw a diagram of the demand for this grower's maize, with his supply, to show perfectly elastic demand and the effect of the bigger harvest, and explain what it shows.
items.canonical_answer: Price (N$ a tonne) goes on the vertical axis and tonnes on the horizontal. Demand for his maize, D, is a horizontal line at N$5 000: at any higher price quantity demanded falls to zero, so PED is infinite. His supply S1 crosses D at E1, 40 tonnes. The rains shift supply right to S2, crossing D at E2: 60 tonnes, still at N$5 000. The diagram shows the whole change landing on quantity: the price does not move, and his revenue rises from N$200 000 to N$300 000.
marking_guidance: Axes labelled: price (N$ a tonne) on the vertical axis and quantity (tonnes) on the horizontal.
Original curves drawn and labelled: a horizontal demand curve D at N$5 000, crossed by S1 at E1, 40 tonnes.
The shift or movement, in the correct direction: the rains shift supply right from S1 to S2, moving the market along the horizontal demand curve.
New equilibrium marked and labelled at E2, 60 tonnes at N$5 000.
What the diagram shows, in words: perfectly elastic demand, PED infinite, so the change falls wholly on quantity and the price stays at N$5 000.

The link between the horizontal curve and the outcome - buyers who take any quantity at N$5 000 and none above it - and the consequence, 20 more tonnes sold and N$100 000 more revenue, carry the analysis marks.

items.prompt: A taxi association in Rundu cuts the fare on a town route from N$15 to N$12, and trips rise from 2 000 to 2 200 a week. Using the figures, explain what the fare cut does to total spending on trips, and why.
items.canonical_answer: The fare fell by 3 / 15 x 100 = 20 per cent, while trips rose by 200 / 2000 x 100 = 10 per cent, so PED = 10 / 20 = 0.5: demand is price-inelastic. Total spending falls from 15 x 2000 = 30000 to 12 x 2200 = 26400, a loss of N$3 600 a week, because the percentage rise in trips is smaller than the percentage cut in the fare. Therefore cutting the price where demand is inelastic lowers total spending.
marking_guidance: Context: the data - the fare cut from N$15 to N$12 and trips up from 2 000 to 2 200 - must be used to find PED = 0.5.
Reasoning: because quantity demanded rose by a smaller percentage than the fare fell, the lower fare on every trip outweighs the extra trips.
Conclusion: therefore total spending falls from N$30 000 to N$26 400, as a price cut does where demand is inelastic.

items.prompt: Explain why total spending on a good stays the same when its price changes, if the price elasticity of demand for the good is exactly 1.
items.canonical_answer: With PED = 1, the percentage change in quantity demanded equals the percentage change in price, in the opposite direction. So when the price rises, the gain from charging more for each unit is offset by the loss from selling fewer units. Total spending, price multiplied by quantity, therefore stays the same; on a diagram the spending rectangle under the new point has the same area as the one under the old. This differs from inelastic demand, where a rise increases spending, and elastic demand, where it reduces spending.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: how the two changes interact - because the percentage change in quantity demanded equals the percentage change in price, the gain per unit offsets the units lost.

Consequence: therefore total spending (price x quantity) is unchanged, and the spending rectangles have equal areas; a contrast with inelastic or elastic demand earns credit only once the mechanism is stated.

items.prompt: A household in Katutura spends N$600 a month on electricity and N$300 on soft drinks. Both prices rise by 20%. Its demand for electricity is price-inelastic, while its demand for soft drinks is price-elastic because water and juice are close substitutes. Explain what PED means for the household's decisions after the price rises.
items.canonical_answer: Electricity demand is price-inelastic, so quantity falls by a smaller percentage than the 20% price rise and spending is likely to increase. If usage did not change at all, the bill would be N$600 x 1.20 = N$720; that is an illustration, not the exact new bill. Soft drinks have close substitutes, so the household reduces purchases more strongly and spending is likely to fall. The exact bills cannot be calculated without the new quantities. PED helps the household identify where substitution is easier.
marking_guidance: Context: use electricity spending of N$600 and soft-drink spending of N$300 with the 20% price rises.
Reasoning: because quantities respond differently, substitution and spending effects differ; the exact new quantities are not supplied.
Conclusion: N$720 illustrates unchanged electricity usage, not a calculated inelastic-demand bill.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Which best defines price elasticity of demand?
A  the change in quantity demanded when any influence on demand changes
B  the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the good's own price
C  the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price
D  the total amount consumers spend on a good at one price

2. A price rises from N$8 to N$10 and quantity demanded falls from 150 to 120 units. PED is:
A  0.80
B  1.25
C  5.0
D  30.0

3. Demand is price-inelastic when:
A  PED is greater than 1
B  quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price
C  PED lies between 0 and 1
D  the demand curve is flatter than the supply curve

4. A good with several close substitutes on the same shelf tends to have:
A  elastic demand, because buyers can switch when the price rises
B  inelastic demand, because buyers stay loyal to the good
C  unit elasticity at every price
D  no measurable elasticity

5. Total spending on a good equals:
A  price plus quantity
B  price multiplied by quantity sold
C  price divided by quantity
D  quantity demanded at the average price

6. Where demand is price-inelastic, a rise in the good's price tends to:
A  lower total spending, because buyers leave the market in large numbers
B  raise total spending, because quantity demanded falls by a smaller percentage than the price rose
C  leave total spending unchanged
D  raise total spending only where the good is a luxury

7. Which purchase is likely to carry the most price-inelastic demand?
A  a specific brand of bottled water beside five others
B  a week's medicine from the only clinic pharmacy in Gobabis
C  a luxury holiday at a lodge near Etosha
D  a restaurant dinner that can be skipped this week

8. A seller raises price and revenue falls. The most specific conclusion is that:
A  demand is price-elastic
B  the seller's costs must have risen
C  demand was price-inelastic, but not enough
D  the supply of the good fell
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 A, 3 C, 4 A, 5 B, 6 B, 7 B, 8 A.
1. B is the definition - responsiveness of quantity demanded to the good's own price. A lets any influence count, which is the shift of demand from topic 2.3, not elasticity; C is the supply-side twin from topic 2.8; D is total spending, a level, not a responsiveness.
2. A: the percentage fall in quantity demanded is 20.0 per cent, since 30 / 150 x 100 = 20, and the percentage rise in price is 25.0 per cent, since 2 / 8 x 100 = 25, so PED is 20 / 25 = 0.80. B divides the other way round, price over quantity; C subtracts instead of dividing percentages; D is the raw change in units, not a percentage comparison.
3. C is the classification: PED between 0 and 1 means quantity demanded moves less, in percentage terms, than price. A reverses the classification; B describes elastic demand; D compares shapes across curves that belong to different sides of the market.
4. A: close substitutes give buyers a way out, so demand tends to be elastic. B holds only where buyers cannot switch, the opposite case; C mistakes a single stretch for the whole curve; D assumes elasticity cannot be measured, when the whole topic is its measurement.
5. B is the formula: price times quantity sold, which is also the seller's revenue. A adds quantities that already live in different units; C divides the wrong way; D describes a point on a curve, not a total.
6. B: with inelastic demand the percentage fall in quantity demanded is smaller, so the higher price wins on the multiplication. A describes elastic demand; C is the borderline unit case, not the general inelastic one; D gets the determinant backwards - luxuries lean elastic, not inelastic.
7. B: clinic medicine is a necessity with no substitute at hand, the most inelastic of the four. A has the closest substitutes, so it leans elastic; C and D are luxuries or postponables, which lean elastic.
8. A: revenue falling after a rise is the signature of elastic demand - the percentage fall in quantity demanded outweighed the percentage rise in price. B brings in costs, which affect profit rather than revenue; C is a contradiction, since inelastic demand is exactly the case where the rise pays; D is a supply-side story about the seller, not the buyers whose behaviour the revenue fall records.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question, eight in total; the correct option for each is listed and every distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Each distractor traces to a named error: the shift of demand confused with elasticity, the percentage division taken upside down, the classification reversed, substitutes held to build loyalty, total spending mistaken for a level, the wrong determinant named, and a revenue fall read as a cost story.

items.prompt:
A newspaper report from Windhoek, October 2026: "Rooibos tea from a single Windhoek trader was the market's quiet winner this winter. The trader sold 800 packets in March at N$25 each; by July, after a poor harvest, the price stood at N$35 and sales were 720 packets. Shoppers told this paper the tea is the one warm drink their households will not give up. A manager at the trader said a bottled iced-tea alternative had just arrived on the next shelf at N$18."

Table 1 - Windhoek rooibos packets
  price per packet: N$25 in March, N$35 in July
  packets sold: 800 in March, 720 in July
  substitutes on the shelf: none in March, one bottled alternative at N$18 in July
  shoppers' view: a drink their households will not give up

(a) Calculate the percentage change in the price of a packet between March and July. [1]
(b) Identify from Table 1 two determinants of price elasticity of demand that apply to rooibos packets. [2]
(c) Explain whether the demand for rooibos packets is price-elastic or price-inelastic over these prices, using the figures. [4]
(d) Analyse what the figures suggest will happen to the trader's revenue if the poor harvest pushes the price higher still, using the data as evidence. Consider at least one reason why the outcome may differ from what the figures suggest. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) 40.0 per cent, since 10 / 25 x 100 = 40.
(b) The availability of substitutes - none on the shelf in March, a bottled iced-tea alternative at N$18 in July; and whether the good is a necessity - shoppers call it a drink their households will not give up.
(c) The percentage fall in quantity demanded was 10.0 per cent, since 80 / 800 x 100 = 10, against the 40.0 per cent price rise, so PED is 10 / 40 = 0.25. Because 0.25 lies between 0 and 1, demand for the packets over these prices is price-inelastic: quantity demanded moved far less, in percentage terms, than the price did. The figures fit the table's determinants - a drink households treat as a necessity, with no substitute on the shelf in March - and the revenue movement confirms the classification: total spending rose from N$20 000, since 25 x 800 = 20000, to N$25 200, since 35 x 720 = 25200, the direction an inelastic market produces when price rises.
(d) With demand inelastic over the range measured, a further price rise tends to raise the trader's revenue again, since the percentage fall in packets is likely to stay below the percentage rise in price. The evidence is the 0.25 figure and the revenue rise from N$20 000 to N$25 200 already recorded, with shoppers calling the tea a drink their households will not give up. However, the figure was measured over a market with no substitute, and Table 1 records that a bottled alternative at N$18 has just arrived on the next shelf - the substitutes determinant changing tends to make demand more elastic than 0.25 says, so the next rise works on a different market from the last. The time determinant points the same way: responsiveness tends to grow as shoppers adjust to the alternative. On the other hand, if the bottled iced tea proves a poor match for hot rooibos in winter, the substitute stays distant and demand may stay inelastic enough for the rise to keep paying - the outcome depends on how close buyers judge the alternative, which the March figures cannot show.
marking_guidance: Parts (a) and (b) are read from the data; the six-mark part must use the figures as evidence - the 40.0 per cent rise, the 10.0 per cent fall, the 0.25, the two revenue totals - not as analysis itself.
One mark per distinct linked statement in (c): the two percentage changes, the division, the classification, and the revenue confirmation each earn only when the link to the next is made.
Part (d) is marked on expected relationship, then evidence, then analysis, then an exception; quoting figures without the relationship they support earns nothing.
For whom: consequences must be named for the trader, whose revenue is at stake, and the shoppers, whose weekly spending on the tea rises with the price.

facts: price N$25 to N$35, packets 800 to 720
substitute: none in March, one at N$18 in July
shoppers call the tea a necessity

items.prompt:
A charcoal trader supplies households in Otavi. Answer all parts.

(a) Define price elasticity of demand. [2]
(b) Explain, for a household choosing charcoal, how the availability of substitutes and the share of income a purchase takes determine the elasticity of demand for a good. [4]
(c) The trader sells 500 bags of charcoal a month at N$60 a bag. It raises the price to N$66 and sells 475 bags. The town's electricity supplier, meanwhile, cut its price last year and the charcoal trader lost 25 bags a month of sales at the old price. Analyse what these figures mean for the trader's revenue and for the households of Otavi. [6]
(d) Discuss whether a seller with price-inelastic demand should keep raising its price. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in its own price.
(b) Substitutes: where close alternatives are easy to switch to, a price rise tends to push buyers towards them, so demand tends to be price-elastic; with no close substitute, buyers have no way out and demand tends to be inelastic. Share of income: a purchase that takes a small slice of the household budget tends to carry inelastic demand, because even a large percentage price rise changes weekly spending little, while a purchase that takes a large slice - and can be postponed - tends to carry elastic demand. Each determinant works the same way: it decides how easily the buyer can leave the good behind when its price rises.
(c) The change is the trader's own price rise from N$60 to N$66, a 10.0 per cent rise, since 6 / 60 x 100 = 10, with quantity demanded falling from 500 to 475 bags, a 5.0 per cent fall, since 25 / 500 x 100 = 5. PED is 5 / 10 = 0.5, so demand for charcoal at these prices is price-inelastic. Because the percentage fall in bags stays below the percentage rise in price, this causes total revenue to rise, from N$30 000, since 60 x 500 = 30000, to N$31 350, since 66 x 475 = 31350. For the firm, revenue rises by N$1 350, since 31350 - 30000 = 1350; for the consumer, the households that keep buying pay more for the same warmth, so their other spending is squeezed. The electricity cut is the exception that proves the determinant: electricity is a substitute for charcoal in cooking and heating, so its cheaper price pulled 25 bags a month of demand away at the old price - the substitute working on the demand curve, topic 2.3's shift, underneath the elasticity the trader measured.
(d) Why it might: with inelastic demand, each rise tends to raise revenue, since the percentage fall in quantity demanded stays smaller than the percentage rise in price - the Otavi figures, where a 10.0 per cent rise cost only 5.0 per cent of bags, show exactly that. The rise is therefore tempting, and for a seller facing inelastic demand it pays, in revenue terms, each time the figure holds. Why it might not: three limits bound the policy. First, elasticity moves along the curve - demand curves tend to hold elastic stretches at higher prices, so rises that pay at N$66 may stop paying further up, and each rise travels towards the stretch where buyers respond sharply. Second, the determinants drift - the electricity cut shows substitutes arriving and changing the market, and responsiveness grows with time as households adjust, so today's inelastic figure may be elastic by the next rise. Third, revenue is not profit: rising revenue settles nothing about profit until costs are known, and a seller with rising costs may find the extra revenue absorbed before it becomes profit. Judgement: on balance the seller should not read inelastic demand as a licence for unlimited rises, because the policy pays only while the figure holds, and each rise both tests and erodes it. The condition it depends on: the measured PED at the new price staying below 1 - the seller that checks the figure each time may keep rising for a while; the seller that raises blindly stops being an inelastic seller exactly when its market finds a substitute.
marking_guidance: Every part carries a model answer; part (d) is level-marked over three bands.
(a) rewards the precise definition: responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the good's own price.
(b) one mark per distinct determinant with its mechanism: substitutes through the way out, income share through the size of the sacrifice - each with the link made.

(c) one mark per distinct linked statement from the starting point - the two percentage changes and the 0.5 - through the mechanism, the revenue rise from N$30 000 to N$31 350, to the consequence for the trader and the households, with the electricity cut read as the substitute shifting demand beneath the elasticity.

(d) Level 3 examines why it might - each rise paying while the figure holds - and why it might not - elasticity moving along the curve, determinants drifting, revenue not being profit - and reaches a judgement naming the condition it depends on: the PED at the new price staying below 1. Level 2 develops one side; Level 1 asserts.

facts: charcoal: 500 bags at N$60, then 475 at N$66
electricity price cut last year cost 25 bags a month at the old price

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "The government of a country is considering a new indirect tax on sugary drinks. Discuss whether the tax is likely to meet both of its aims: raising revenue and reducing consumption." Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for the tax meeting its aims: the two aims sit on the same determinant. Sugary drinks are a small-share, everyday purchase for many households, so demand tends to be price-inelastic - which serves the revenue aim, because quantity demanded falls little when the tax pushes the price up and the tax keeps collecting on almost every bottle sold.
Chain 1: tax raises the price -> with inelastic demand, the percentage fall in bottles stays below the percentage rise in price -> revenue flows to the government -> the aim of raising money is met (for the government, the consumer who keeps buying).
Second case for: where households treat the drinks as a habit with no ready substitute, the inelastic figure holds both at once, and the revenue aim is met reliably.
Case against, first point: the aims pull against each other through elasticity. A good whose demand is inelastic is a poor target for behaviour change - the same small percentage fall in quantity demanded that makes the revenue reliable makes the consumption reduction barely material, so one of the two aims fails whenever the other succeeds.
Chain 2: demand is inelastic -> tax raises price -> quantity demanded falls by a small percentage -> revenue aim met -> consumption aim largely missed (the aim of reducing consumption is unmet).
Case against, second point: the determinants drift with time. Substitutes arrive - untaxed squashes, water bottles, cross-border shopping - and responsiveness grows as households adjust, so the inelastic figure the plan was built on tends to erode, pushing the tax towards elastic ground where revenue falls away even as consumption finally responds.
Judgement: on balance the tax is likely to meet the revenue aim first and the consumption aim later, if at all - the two aims succeed in the order elasticity allows. The condition it depends on: how elastic demand for sugary drinks proves over time and across substitutes - what settles it is the measured PED of the taxed drinks, checked after the substitutes have had time to arrive.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the structure with the stated judgement is what is assessed.

The plan must carry the case for and the case against, each developed as a chain from tax through elasticity to the aim affected, and name the parties - the government, the consumer, the households whose budgets carry the tax.
The judgement must be decisive and name the condition it depends on: the measured PED over time.
What settles it: whether demand for the taxed drinks proves elastic or inelastic once substitutes arrive - the same figure answers both aims, in opposite directions.
